nodes.name: Probability space and risky asset
nodes.statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a complete 
probability space carrying one risky asset which we denote by $S=(S_k)_{0\leq k\leq n}$ where 
$n\in\mathbb N$ is a fixed finite time horizon.

nodes.name: Zero-interest bank account
nodes.statement:
We assume that the investor has a bank account that,
for simplicity, bears no interest.

nodes.name: i.i.d. Gaussian stock increments
nodes.statement:
We assume that the initial stock price $S_0$ is a known constant 
and the stock increments 
$X_k:=S_k-S_{k-1}$, $k=1,...,n$ are i.i.d. normal variables with mean $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and 
variance equal to $\sigma^2$ for some $\sigma>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Initial price $S_0$ is known; increments $X_k=S_k-S_{k-1}$ are i.i.d. $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$.

nodes.name: Delay of D trading times
nodes.statement:
We fix a nonnegative integer number ${D}\in\mathbb Z_{+}$ and consider a situation where
there is a delay of ${D}$ trading times.

nodes.name: Delay shorter than horizon
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality we assume that ${D}<n$.

nodes.name: Delayed information filtration
nodes.statement:
Hence, the investor's flow of information is given by the filtration 
$\mathcal G_k:=\sigma\left\{S_0,...,S_{\left(k-{D}\right)\vee 0}\right\}$, $k=0,1,...,n$.

nodes.name: Semistatic hedging setup
nodes.statement:
We consider the following semistatic hedging setup.
There are two investment opportunities.
One is trading dynamically the stock at times $0,1,...,n-1$
 and the other is taking a static position in $S_n$, i.e. for any continuous function $f:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R$
 we can buy an option with the random payoff $f(S_n)$ for the amount $\int f d\hat\nu$ where $\hat\nu$ is a given measure (determined by the market).
nodes.statement_short: Investor trades the stock dynamically at times $0,\dots,n-1$ and buys any static payoff $f(S_n)$ at price $\int f d\hat\nu$.

nodes.name: Normal pricing measure
nodes.statement: We assume that $\hat\nu$ is a normal distribution.

nodes.name: No-arbitrage forces mean of pricing measure
nodes.statement:
Observe that 
the market allows to buy one stock for the price $S_0$ and so, in order to avoid an obvious arbitrage we should require 
$\int z d\hat\nu(z)=S_0$.

nodes.name: Pricing measure N(S_0, n hat-sigma^2)
nodes.statement: Hence, we assume that $\hat\nu=\mathcal N(S_0, n\hat\sigma^2)$ for some $\hat\sigma>0$.

nodes.name: Trading strategy (discrete semistatic)
nodes.statement:
Formally, a trading strategy is a pair $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ where $\gamma=(\gamma_1,...,\gamma_n)$ is a predictable process with respect
to $\{\mathcal G_k\}_{k=0}^n$ and $f:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R$ is a continuous function such that 
$\int |f| d\hat\nu<\infty$.
differentia: $\gamma=(\gamma_1,...,\gamma_n)$ is a predictable process with respect to $\{\mathcal G_k\}_{k=0}^n$
$f:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R$ is a continuous function such that $\int |f| d\hat\nu<\infty$

nodes.name: Set of trading strategies A
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal A$ the set of all trading strategies.

nodes.name: Terminal portfolio value V_n
nodes.statement:
For $\pi=(\gamma,f)\in\mathcal A$ the corresponding portfolio value
at the maturity date is given by 
\begin{equation} V^{\pi}_n=f(S_n)+\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma_i X_i-\int fd\hat\nu.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Portfolio value (eq:value)
nodes.statement: V^{\pi}_n=f(S_n)+\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma_i X_i-\int fd\hat\nu.
nodes.label: eq:value

nodes.name: Equivalence of trading strategies (discrete)
nodes.statement: We say that two trading strategies $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent if there exists a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $\gamma-\tilde\gamma\equiv c$ and $\tilde f-f$ is a linear function with slope equal to $c$. Clearly if $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent then $V^{\pi}_n=V^{\tilde\pi}_n$. Let us argue that the opposite direction also holds. Indeed, let $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ be two trading strategies such that $V^{\pi}_n=V^{\tilde\pi}_n$. Then, from (\ref{eq:value}) we obtain that the random variable $f(S_n)-\tilde f(S_n)+\left(\gamma_{n}-\tilde\gamma_{n}\right)S_n$ is measurable with respect to $\sigma\{S_0,...,S_{n-1}\}$. Since the support of $S_n$ given $\sigma\{S_0,...,S_{n-1}\}$ contains more than two values (it is all the real line) we conclude that $f-\tilde f$ is a linear function and so $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: Two strategies give the same terminal value iff their stock positions differ by a constant $c$ and their payoffs by a linear function of slope $c$.
nodes.label: rem2

nodes.name: Equivalent trading strategies
nodes.statement:
We say that two trading strategies $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent if there exists a constant
$c\in\mathbb R$ such that $\gamma-\tilde\gamma\equiv c$ and 
$\tilde f-f$ is a linear function with slope equal to $c$.

nodes.name: Equivalent strategies iff equal terminal value
nodes.statement:
Clearly if $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent
then $V^{\pi}_n=V^{\tilde\pi}_n$. Let us argue that the opposite direction also holds.
conclusions:
Clearly if $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent
then $V^{\pi}_n=V^{\tilde\pi}_n$. Let us argue that the opposite direction also holds.

nodes.name: Proof that equal values imply equivalence
nodes.statement:
Indeed, let 
$\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ be two trading strategies 
such that $V^{\pi}_n=V^{\tilde\pi}_n$. Then, from (\ref{eq:value}) we obtain that the random variable 
$f(S_n)-\tilde f(S_n)+\left(\gamma_{n}-\tilde\gamma_{n}\right)S_n$ is 
 measurable with respect to $\sigma\{S_0,...,S_{n-1}\}$. Since the support of $S_n$ given 
 $\sigma\{S_0,...,S_{n-1}\}$ contains more than two values (it is all the real line) we conclude that 
 $f-\tilde f$ is a linear function and so $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: Conditioning on $S_0,\dots,S_{n-1}$: $f-\tilde f$ plus a linear term is measurable, and full support of $S_n$ forces $f-\tilde f$ linear.

nodes.name: Exponential utility maximization (discrete delayed semistatic)
nodes.statement:
Next, the investor’s preferences are described by an exponential utility function 
$u(x)=-\exp(- x)$, $x\in\mathbb R$
and her goal is to
\begin{equation} \mbox{Maximize} \ \ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_n\right)\right] \ \ \mbox{over} \ \ \pi\in\mathcal A
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}$ denotes the expectation with respect to the 
market probability measure $\mathbb P$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[-\exp(-V^\pi_n)]$ over semistatic strategies $\pi\in\mathcal A$ with delayed information.

nodes.name: Utility maximization objective (1.2)
nodes.statement: \mbox{Maximize} \ \ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_n\right)\right] \ \ \mbox{over} \ \ \pi\in\mathcal A

nodes.name: Unit risk aversion without loss of generality
nodes.statement:
Clearly, 
for any portfolio strategy 
$\pi$ and a constant $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, 
$V^{\lambda\pi}_n=\lambda V^{\pi}_n$. 
Thus, without loss of generality, we take 
the absolute risk aversion parameter to be equal $1$.

nodes.name: Explicit solution of delayed semistatic exponential utility maximization (discrete time)
nodes.statement: Fix $n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma$. Let \begin{equation} a:=\begin{cases} \frac{\sigma^2}{2n\hat\sigma^2}+\frac{\sqrt{\left(2D+1-\frac{D(D+1)\sigma^2}{n\hat\sigma^2}\right)^2- 4 (D+1)D \left(1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}\right)}-2D-1}{2 D (D+1)}, & \text{if \ $D\neq 0$}\\ \frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}-1, & \text{if \ $D=0$} \end{cases} \end{equation} and define the sequence $\{b_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ by recursion ($D>0$) \begin{equation} b_1=...=b_{D}=a, \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ b_i=\frac{a }{a D+1} \sum_{j=1}^{D} b_{i-j}\ \ \mbox{for} \ \ i>D, \end{equation} for $D=0$ we set $b_i=0$ for all $i>0$. Then, $a>-\frac{1}{D+1}$ and so, the above sequence is well defined. The maximizer $\pi^{*}=(\gamma^{*},f^{*})$ for the optimization problem (\ref{1.2}) is unique (up to equivalency) and is given by \begin{equation} \gamma^{*}_i=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} (b_{i-j}-a) X_{j} \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ f^{*}(S_n):=\frac{a}{2\sigma^2}(S_n-S_0)^2. \end{equation} The corresponding value is given by \begin{align} u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma) &:=\sup_{\pi\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_n\right)\right]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi^*}_n\right)\right]\nonumber\\ &=-\exp\left(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} n(a\hat\sigma^2-\mu^2)\right) \sqrt{\frac{\big(1+ {D} a\big)^{n-{D}-1}}{\big(1+({D}+1) a\big)^{n-{D}}}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: With i.i.d. Gaussian increments and delay $D$, the optimal strategy is Merton fraction plus a recursively computed linear filter of past increments, with a quadratic static payoff; the value is explicit.
conclusions: $a>-\frac{1}{D+1}$ and so, the above sequence is well defined

The maximizer $\pi^{*}=(\gamma^{*},f^{*})$ for the optimization problem (\ref{1.2}) is unique (up to equivalency) and is given by \begin{equation} \gamma^{*}_i=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} (b_{i-j}-a) X_{j} \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ f^{*}(S_n):=\frac{a}{2\sigma^2}(S_n-S_0)^2. \end{equation}

The corresponding value is given by \begin{align} u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma) &:=\sup_{\pi\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_n\right)\right]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi^*}_n\right)\right]\nonumber\\ &=-\exp\left(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} n(a\hat\sigma^2-\mu^2)\right) \sqrt{\frac{\big(1+ {D} a\big)^{n-{D}-1}}{\big(1+({D}+1) a\big)^{n-{D}}}}. \end{align}
nodes.label: thm1.1

nodes.name: Constant a (eq:a_sol)
nodes.statement: a:=\begin{cases} \frac{\sigma^2}{2n\hat\sigma^2}+\frac{\sqrt{\left(2D+1-\frac{D(D+1)\sigma^2}{n\hat\sigma^2}\right)^2- 4 (D+1)D \left(1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}\right)}-2D-1}{2 D (D+1)}, & \text{if \ $D\neq 0$}\\ \frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}-1, & \text{if \ $D=0$} \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq:a_sol

nodes.name: Recursion for b_i (1.4)
nodes.statement: b_1=...=b_{D}=a, \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ b_i=\frac{a }{a D+1} \sum_{j=1}^{D} b_{i-j}\ \ \mbox{for} \ \ i>D,

nodes.name: Optimal strategy (1.5)
nodes.statement: \gamma^{*}_i=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} (b_{i-j}-a) X_{j} \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ f^{*}(S_n):=\frac{a}{2\sigma^2}(S_n-S_0)^2.

nodes.name: Optimal value (1.6)
nodes.statement: u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma) &:=\sup_{\pi\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_n\right)\right]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi^*}_n\right)\right]\nonumber\\ &=-\exp\left(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} n(a\hat\sigma^2-\mu^2)\right) \sqrt{\frac{\big(1+ {D} a\big)^{n-{D}-1}}{\big(1+({D}+1) a\big)^{n-{D}}}}.

nodes.name: Financial interpretation of the optimal strategy
nodes.statement:
Let us briefly collect some financial-economic observations from this result. First,
Theorem \ref{thm1.1} states that the optimal trading strategy $\gamma^{*}$
is a sum of the well known
Merton fraction $\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}$ and a centered discrete-time Gaussian process which we compute 
by recursive relations. 
The static option $f^{*}(S_T)$ is given by a quadratic payoff function.

nodes.name: No mispricing gives the Merton strategy
nodes.statement:
Observe that for the case $\sigma=\hat\sigma$ we have $a=0$
and the optimal strategy is to hold $\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}$ stocks (the well known Merton fraction) and not invest in static options. The corresponding value is 
$u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\sigma)=-\exp\left(-\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$
conclusions:
we have $a=0$
and the optimal strategy is to hold $\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}$ stocks (the well known Merton fraction) and not invest in static options. The corresponding value is 
$u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\sigma)=-\exp\left(-\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$

nodes.name: Value without delay (D=0)
nodes.statement:
First, for $D=0$ (i.e. no delay) we have 
$a=\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}-1$ and the value is given by 
$$u(n,0,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)=-\exp\left(-\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{n g\left(\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}\right)}{2}\right)$$
where 
$g(z):=z-\log z-1$, $z>0$.
nodes.statement_short: For $D=0$, $a=\sigma^2/\hat\sigma^2-1$ and the value is the Merton value times $\exp(-n g(\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2)/2)$ with $g(z)=z-\log z-1$.
conclusions:
we have 
$a=\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}-1$ and the value is given by 
$$u(n,0,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)=-\exp\left(-\frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{n g\left(\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}\right)}{2}\right)$$
where 
$g(z):=z-\log z-1$, $z>0$.

nodes.name: Properties of g(z)=z-log z-1
nodes.statement:
The function $g\geq 0$ is convex and attains its minimal value (equal to zero) at $z=1$. This function 
also appears in the Brownian setup 
when dealing with a scaling limit of relative entropies associated with appropriate time discretizations 
of Brownian martingale and Brownian motion, for details see \cite{backhoff2023most} and the references therein.

nodes.name: a is the largest root of the quadratic (equat)
nodes.statement:
For general $D$ and $\sigma\neq\hat\sigma$ we will see in Section \ref{sec:3} that $a$
is the largest (real) root of the quadratic equation (\ref{equat}).
conclusions:
For general $D$ and $\sigma\neq\hat\sigma$ we will see in Section \ref{sec:3} that $a$
is the largest (real) root of the quadratic equation (\ref{equat}).

nodes.name: Sign of a via Vieta's formulas
nodes.statement:
If $\hat\sigma>\sigma$ 
and $D>0$ then the sum of the roots of the quadratic equation 
(\ref{equat}) is 
$\frac{\frac{D(D+1)\sigma^2}{n\hat\sigma^2}-2D-1}{D(D+1)}<0$ and the product of the roots is 
$\frac{1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}}{D(D+1)}>0$. Hence, in this case both of the roots are negative, and in particular $a<0$.
Namely, the investor short sells the quadratic option $(S_n-S_0)^2$. 
For the case $\sigma>\hat\sigma$ the product of the roots is 
$\frac{1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}}{D(D+1)}<0$, and so the large root $a$ is positive.
nodes.statement_short: Vieta's formulas for (equat): both roots negative when $\hat\sigma>\sigma$, product negative (so largest root positive) when $\sigma>\hat\sigma$.

nodes.name: Sign of a matches sign of sigma - hat sigma
nodes.statement: Next, fix $n,D,\mu,\sigma$. In view of the above we have $a>0\Leftrightarrow\sigma>\hat\sigma$.
conclusions: Next, fix $n,D,\mu,\sigma$. In view of the above we have $a>0\Leftrightarrow\sigma>\hat\sigma$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of the value in hat sigma
nodes.statement:
Hence, 
the value function 
$u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)$ as a function of $\hat\sigma$ is increasing for $\hat\sigma>\sigma$ and decreasing for $\hat\sigma<\sigma$.
conclusions:
Hence, 
the value function 
$u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)$ as a function of $\hat\sigma$ is increasing for $\hat\sigma>\sigma$ and decreasing for $\hat\sigma<\sigma$.

nodes.name: Proof of monotonicity in hat sigma
nodes.statement:
Indeed, let $\sigma<\hat\sigma_1<\hat\sigma_2$
and let $\pi^{*}_{\hat\sigma_1}$ be the optimal portfolio for $\hat\sigma=\hat\sigma_1$. Since the corresponding static option
is $\frac{a}{2\sigma^2}(S_n-S_0)^2$ with $a<0$, then the value (at the maturity date) of the same portfolio for the case $\hat\sigma=\hat\sigma_2$ will be larger.
Similarly, if $\hat\sigma_1<\hat\sigma_2<\sigma$ and $\pi^{*}_{\hat\sigma_2}$ is the optimal portfolio for $\hat\sigma=\hat\sigma_2$ then due to the fact that the corresponding 
$a$ is positive, the value of the same portfolio for the case $\hat\sigma=\hat\sigma_1$ will be larger.
nodes.statement_short: Keep the optimal portfolio for one $\hat\sigma$ and use the sign of $a$: the same portfolio does better at the other $\hat\sigma$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic arbitrage for extreme hat sigma
nodes.statement: Finally, we argue that there is an asymptotic arbitrage for the case where $\hat\sigma$ is very large or very small.
conclusions: Finally, we argue that there is an asymptotic arbitrage for the case where $\hat\sigma$ is very large or very small.

nodes.name: Static-hedging proof of asymptotic arbitrage
nodes.statement:
To this end, instead of applying Theorem \ref{thm1.1}, we provide a straightforward argument based on static hedging.
Indeed, by 
taking $\gamma\equiv 0$ and $f(S_n)=\frac{1}{\hat\sigma}(S_n-S_0)^2$ it follows that
\begin{equation} \lim_{\hat\sigma\rightarrow 0} u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)=0 
\end{equation}
and by taking 
 $\gamma\equiv 0$ and $f(S_n)=-\frac{1}{\hat\sigma}(S_n-S_0)^2$
we obtain 
\begin{equation} \lim_{\hat\sigma\rightarrow \infty} u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)=0.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Static hedge only: take $\gamma\equiv 0$ and $f=\pm(S_n-S_0)^2/\hat\sigma$, giving value tending to 0 as $\hat\sigma\to 0$ or $\infty$.

nodes.name: Limit as hat sigma -> 0 (static1)
nodes.statement: \lim_{\hat\sigma\rightarrow 0} u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)=0
nodes.label: static1

nodes.name: Limit as hat sigma -> infinity (static2)
nodes.statement: \lim_{\hat\sigma\rightarrow \infty} u(n,D,\mu,\sigma,\hat\sigma)=0.
nodes.label: static2

nodes.name: Set Q of delayed martingale measures consistent with prices
nodes.statement:
Denote by $\mathcal Q$ the set of all equivalent probability measures $\mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P$ with finite entropy 
 $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]<\infty$ relative to $\mathbb P$ that satisfy 
 \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[S_j-S_i|\mathcal G_i]=0 \ \ \forall j\geq i
 \end{equation}
 and $(S_n;\mathbb Q) \sim \hat\nu$ (the latter means that the distribution of $S_n$ under $\mathbb Q$
 is equal to $\hat\nu$).
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal Q$: finite-entropy equivalent measures under which $S$ is a martingale w.r.t. the delayed filtration and $S_n\sim\hat\nu$.

nodes.name: Delayed martingale condition (2.0)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[S_j-S_i|\mathcal G_i]=0 \ \ \forall j\geq i

nodes.name: Verification lemma for semistatic exponential utility
nodes.statement: If a triplet $(\tilde\pi,\tilde{\mathbb Q},C)\in \mathcal A\times \mathcal Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfies \begin{equation} V^{\tilde\pi}_n+\log\left(\frac{d{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)=C \end{equation} then $\tilde\pi\in\mathcal A$ is the unique (up to equivalency) optimal portfolio for the optimization problem (\ref{1.2}) and the corresponding value is $ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\tilde\pi}_n\right)\right]=-e^{-C}.$
nodes.statement_short: If $V^{\tilde\pi}_n+\log(d\tilde Q/dP)$ is constant $C$ for some $\tilde Q\in\mathcal Q$, then $\tilde\pi$ is the unique optimizer with value $-e^{-C}$.
assumptions: a triplet $(\tilde\pi,\tilde{\mathbb Q},C)\in \mathcal A\times \mathcal Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfies \begin{equation} V^{\tilde\pi}_n+\log\left(\frac{d{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)=C \end{equation}
conclusions: $\tilde\pi\in\mathcal A$ is the unique (up to equivalency) optimal portfolio for the optimization problem (\ref{1.2}) and the corresponding value is $ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\tilde\pi}_n\right)\right]=-e^{-C}.$
nodes.label: lem2.1

nodes.name: Verification identity (2.1)
nodes.statement: V^{\tilde\pi}_n+\log\left(\frac{d{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)=C

Thus, using similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma 2.1 in \cite{BD:2021} we obtain (in view of (ef{2.0})) that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma_i X_iight]=0$. This together with (ef{2.3}) yields (ef{2.2}) and completes the first step. \ ${}$\ 	extbf{Step II:} We proceed using similar arguments to those in Step II of the proof of Theorem $1.1$ in \cite{dolinsky2023exponential}. From (ef{2.1})--(ef{2.2}) for $\pi:=	ilde\pi$ we obtain  egin{equation} \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{	ilde \pi}_night)ight] ight)=-C=- \mathbb E_{	ilde{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left( rac{d	ilde{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight]. \end{equation} Next, it is well known that for a strictly concave utility maximization problem, the optimal portfolio value is unique (if exists) and so in view of Remark ef{rem2} and (ef{2.5}), in order to complete the proof of the Lemma it remains to show that in general we have the inequality  egin{equation} \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_night)ight] ight)\geq -\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left( rac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight] \ \  orall (\pi,\mathbb Q)\in\mathcal A	imes\mathcal Q. \end{equation} Let us establish (ef{2.6}). We assume that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_night)ight]<\infty$ (otherwise (ef{2.6}) is trivial). Then for any $z\geq 0$  egin{align*} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_night)ight] &=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_night)+z  rac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}V^{\pi}_night]\ &\geq \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[z rac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\left(1-\log \left(z rac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight)ight]\ &=z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left( rac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight]. \end{align*} The first equality is due to \eqref{2.2}. The inequality follows from the Legendre-Fenchel duality inequality $xy \leq e^x+y(\log y-1)$ by setting $x=-V^{\pi}_n$ and $y=z rac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}$. The last equality is straightforward. From simple calculus it follows that the concave function $zightarrow z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left( rac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight]$, $z>0$ attains its maximum at $z^{*}:=\exp\left(-\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log \left( rac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight]ight)$ and the corresponding maximal value is also $z^{*}$. This completes the proof of (ef{2.6}).
nodes.statement_short: Duality: Step I shows $\mathbb E_Q[V^\pi_n]=0$ for all $Q\in\mathcal Q$; Step II applies the Legendre-Fenchel inequality and optimizes over a scalar $z$.

nodes.name: Zero expected value under Q (2.2)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[V^{\pi}_n]=0.

nodes.name: Static payoff price (2.3)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} [f(S_n)]=\int f d\hat\nu.

nodes.name: Entropy bound on negative part (2.4)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\left(V^{\pi}_n\right)_{-}\right]\leq \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_n\right)\right]+ \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right] <\infty.

nodes.name: Duality equality (2.5)
nodes.statement: \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\tilde \pi}_n\right)\right] \right)=-C=- \mathbb E_{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d\tilde{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right].

nodes.name: Weak duality inequality (2.6)
nodes.statement: \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_n\right)\right] \right)\geq -\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right] \ \ \forall (\pi,\mathbb Q)\in\mathcal A\times\mathcal Q.

nodes.name: Banded positive definite matrices S_D
nodes.statement:
Let ${\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ be the set 
of all $n \times n$ positive definite matrices $Q$ that satisfy $Q_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|>{D}$. Namely, 
${\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ is the set of all banded positive definite matrices with lower bandwidth and upper bandwidth equal to ${D}$.

nodes.name: Symmetric Toeplitz matrices T_n
nodes.statement: Let ${T}_n$ be the set of all $n \times n$ symmetric Toeplitz matrices.

nodes.name: Toeplitz matrix
nodes.statement: Recall that a Toeplitz matrix is a matrix in which each descending diagonal from left to right is constant.
differentia: each descending diagonal from left to right is constant

nodes.name: Row and column index vectors
nodes.statement:
Let $C$ be a $n \times n$ real matrix and let $I,J \in \{1,..,n\}^k$ be two integer vectors of length $k \leq n$ denoting row and column indices, satisfying $I = (i_1,..,i_k), J=(j_1,..,j_k)$ 
with $1 \leq i_1 < i_2 < .. < i_k \leq n$, $1 \leq j_1 < j_2 < .. < j_k \leq n$.

nodes.name: Minor C_J^I
nodes.statement:
We denote by $C_J^I$ the minor specified by these indices, i.e. 
the determinant of the $k \times k$ sub-matrix determined by taking the elements $C_{ij}$ for $i=i_1,..i_k ; j=j_1,..j_k$.

nodes.name: Index vector [k:l]
nodes.statement: For any two natural numbers $l \geq k$ we denote the vector $(k,k+1,...,l)$ by $[k:l]$.

nodes.name: Toeplitz matrix A has banded inverse and explicit determinant
nodes.statement: Let $\{b_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be the sequence given by (\ref{1.4}). Set $b_0=a+1$ and define the matrix $A\in {T}_n$ by $A_{ij}=b_{|i-j|}$. Then $A^{-1}\in {\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$ and the determinant of $A$ is given by \begin{equation} |A|=\frac{\big(1+({D}+1) a\big)^{n-{D}}}{\big(1+ {D} a\big)^{n-{D}-1}} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The symmetric Toeplitz matrix $A_{ij}=b_{|i-j|}$ (with $b_0=a+1$) has $D$-banded positive definite inverse and an explicit determinant.
assumptions: Let $\{b_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be the sequence given by (\ref{1.4})
Set $b_0=a+1$ and define the matrix $A\in {T}_n$ by $A_{ij}=b_{|i-j|}$
conclusions: $A^{-1}\in {\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$
the determinant of $A$ is given by \begin{equation} |A|=\frac{\big(1+({D}+1) a\big)^{n-{D}}}{\big(1+ {D} a\big)^{n-{D}-1}} . \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem2.2

nodes.name: Proof of banded inverse and determinant of A
nodes.statement: For $D=0$ the statement is trivial. Assume that $D>0$. The proof will be done in three steps. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step I:} In this step we prove that $a$, given by (\ref{eq:a_sol}), satisfies $a>-\frac{1}{D+1}$. Observe that (recall that $D<n$) $$ \lim_{z\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n+z D (D+1)}{\left(Dz+1\right)\left((D+1)z+1\right)}=0 $$ and $$ \lim_{z\downarrow-\frac{1}{D+1}}\frac{n+z D (D+1)}{\left(Dz+1\right)\left((D+1)z+1\right)}=\infty $$ and so, the equation $\frac{n+z D (D+1)}{\left(Dz+1\right)\left((D+1)z+1\right)}=\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}n$ has at least one real root $z> -\frac{1}{D+1}$. Hence, the quadratic equation \begin{equation} D(D+1) z^2+\left(2D+1-\frac{D(D+1)\sigma^2}{n\hat\sigma^2}\right)z+1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}=0 \end{equation} has a real root $z> -\frac{1}{D+1}$. Since $a$ is the largest root of the above quadratic equation it follows that $a\geq z> -\frac{1}{D+1}$. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step II:} In view of the first step, (\ref{1.4}) provides a well defined sequence of real numbers. Hence, $A\in {T}_n$. In this step we show that the matrix $A$ has vanishing sub-$(D+1)$-minors. That is, all minors of the form $A_J^I$ where $I = (i_1,..,i_{D+1}), J=(j_1,..,j_{D+1})$ and $i_i>j_{{D}+1}-{D}$ are equal to zero. Set $b_{-i}:=b_i=a$ for $i=1,..,{D}$. Observe that the sequence $\{b_i\}_{i=-D}^{\infty}$ satisfies the recursion \begin{equation} b_i=\frac{a }{a D+1} \sum_{j=1}^{D} b_{i-j}\ \ \mbox{for} \ \ i>0. \end{equation} Let $A^J_I$ be a sub-$(D+1)$-minor. From the fact that $i_1>j_{D+1}-D$ we obtain that $A_{i_k j_l}=b_{|i_k-j_l|}=b_{i_k-j_l}$. This, together with (\ref{2.8}), yield that all the rows of the matrix that corresponds to the minor $A^J_I$ are determined as linear combinations of rows $i_1,i_1+1,..,i_1+{D}-1$ of $A$, taken at the appropriate columns $j_1,..,j_{{D}+1}$. Hence, the rank of this matrix is at most ${D}$ and $A_J^I=0$ as required. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step III:} In this step we complete the proof. First, for any $m\in\mathbb N$ and $\alpha>-1/m$ define the $m \times m$ matrix $\mathbf {1}^{m,\alpha}$ by $\mathbf {1}^{m,\alpha}_{ij}:=\alpha+\mathbb I_{i=j}$ (as usual $\mathbb I$ denotes the indicator function). Then, for any non-zero vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $x^T \mathbf {1}^{m,\alpha} x = (1+\alpha m) ||x||^2 - \alpha \sum_{i<j} (x_i - x_j)^2 > 0$, hence $\mathbf {1}^{m,\alpha}$ is a positive definite matrix. In addition, the determinant is equal to $ |\mathbf {1}^{m,\alpha}|=1+m\alpha. $ Thus, in view of the second step, from Theorem 5.1 in \cite{BF:81} we obtain that $$ |A|=\frac{\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-{D}} A_{[i:i+{D}]}^{[i:i+{D}]}}{\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n-{D}-1} A_{[i+1:i+{D}]}^{[i+1:i+{D}]}} = \frac{\big(1+({D}+1) a\big)^{n-{D}}}{\big(1+ {D} a\big)^{n-{D}-1}}. $$ Moreover, from Theorem 3.1 in \cite{BF:81}, it follows that $A^{-1}$ is ${D}$-banded. Finally, from the fact that $a>-\frac{1}{D+1}$ we get that that the principal minors $A^{[k+1:k+{D}]}_{[k+1:k+{D}]}>0$ for all $k\leq n-{D}-1$ and $A^{[k:k+{D}]}_{[k:k+{D}]}>0$ for all $k\leq n-{D}$. Hence, by applying Theorem 5.5 in \cite{BF:81} for $r=s={D}+1$ we obtain that $A^{-1}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{{D}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $a>-1/(D+1)$ by the intermediate value theorem; show all sub-$(D+1)$-minors vanish via the recursion; then apply Barrett-Feinsilver theorems on banded inverses.

nodes.name: Quadratic equation for a (equat)
nodes.statement: D(D+1) z^2+\left(2D+1-\frac{D(D+1)\sigma^2}{n\hat\sigma^2}\right)z+1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2}=0
nodes.label: equat

nodes.name: Two-sided recursion for b_i (2.8)
nodes.statement: b_i=\frac{a }{a D+1} \sum_{j=1}^{D} b_{i-j}\ \ \mbox{for} \ \ i>0.

nodes.name: Sum of entries of A^{-1}
nodes.statement: We have $\sum_{i,j=1}^n [A^{-1}]_{ij}=n\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}$.
conclusions: $\sum_{i,j=1}^n [A^{-1}]_{ij}=n\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}$.
nodes.label: lem2.3

nodes.name: Proof of the sum of entries of A^{-1}
nodes.statement: For $D=0$ we have $A^{-1}=\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2} I$ and so, the statement is trivial. Assume that $D>0$. The proof will be done in two steps. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step I:} Set $v=(v_0,...,v_{n-1})$ by \begin{equation} v_0=\frac{a D+1}{a(D+1)+1}, \ \ v_1=...=v_{D}=\frac{-a}{a(D+1)+1}, \ \ v_{D+1}=...=v_{n-1}=0. \end{equation} In this step we prove that \begin{equation} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} v_j b_{|i-j|}=\delta_{i0}, \ \ i=0,1...,n-1. \end{equation} This is shown by straightforward derivation for the different cases of $i$. \\ For $i = 0$: $$ \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} v_j b_{j}=\frac{(1+a)(a{D}+1)}{a ({D}+1)+1} - \frac{{D} a^2}{a ({D}+1)+1} = 1. $$ \noindent For $1 \leq i < {D}$: \begin{align*} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} v_j b_{|i-j|} &= v_0 b_{i}+v_i b_0 +\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} v_j b_{i-j}+\sum_{j=i+1}^{{D}} v_j b_{j-i} \\ &= \frac{a (a D+1)- a(a+1)-a^2 (D-1)}{a({D}+1)+1} = 0. \end{align*} \noindent For $i\geq {D}$: \begin{align*} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} v_j b_{|i-j|} &= \sum_{j=0}^{D} v_j b_{i-j}\\ &= \frac{a D+1}{a({D}+1)+1} \left( b_{i}-\frac{a}{aD+1} \sum_{j=1}^{{D}} b_{i-j}\right)=0 \end{align*} where the last equality follows from the recursive relation in (\ref{1.4}). This completes the first step. \\ ${}$\\ \textbf{Step II:} In this step we complete the proof. From Theorem 1 in \cite{rodman1992inversion} and \eqref{2.15} \begin{equation} [A^{-1}]_{ij}=\frac{1}{v_0}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{i\wedge j} v_{i-k}v_{j-k}-\sum_{k=1}^{i\wedge j-1 }v_{n-i+k}v_{n-j+k}\right). \end{equation} Thus, \begin{align*} \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} [A^{-1}]_{ij} &=\sum_{i=1}^n [A^{-1}]_{ii}+ 2\sum_{k=1}^ D\sum_{j=1}^{n-k} [A^{-1}]_{j+k j}\\ &=n v_0+\frac{v^2_1}{v_0}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \left((i-1)\wedge D-0\vee (D+i-n)\right)\right)\\ &+2 v_1\sum_{k=1}^D (n-k)\\ &+2 \frac{v^2_1}{v_0}\sum_{k=1}^D \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} \left((j-1)\wedge (D-k)-0\vee (D+j-n)\right)\\ &= n v_0+(D-2n-D-1)v_1+D^2 (n-D-1)\frac{v^2_1}{v_0}\\ &=\frac{(a D+1)n}{aD+1+a}-\frac{a D (2n-D-1)}{aD+1+a}+\frac{a^2 D^2 (n-D-1)}{(aD+1)(aD+1+a)}\\ &=n\sigma^2. \end{align*} The first equality is due to the fact that $A^{-1}\in{\mathcal{S}}_D$. The second equality follows from (\ref{2.16}) and the fact that $v_1=...=v_D$ and $v_{D+1}=...=v_{n-1}=0$. The third equality is simple summation. The fourth equality is a substitution of $v_0,v_1$ from (\ref{2.14+}). The last equality is due to the fact that $a>-\frac{1}{D+1}$ is a solution to (\ref{equat}). This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Find the vector $v$ solving the Toeplitz system (2.15) by cases, then apply the Gohberg-Semencul-type inversion formula of Rodman-Shalom and sum the entries.

nodes.name: Inverse formula for A (2.16)
nodes.statement: [A^{-1}]_{ij}=\frac{1}{v_0}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{i\wedge j} v_{i-k}v_{j-k}-\sum_{k=1}^{i\wedge j-1 }v_{n-i+k}v_{n-j+k}\right).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: From Lemma \ref{lem2.2} it follows that the portfolio $\pi^{*}=(\gamma^{*},f^{*})$ which given by (\ref{1.5}) is well defined and, since $b_{i-j}-a=0$ for $i-D-1<j<i$ we have $\pi^{*}\in\mathcal A$. Set \begin{equation} \hat C := \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}n\left(\mu^2-a{\hat\sigma^2}\right) + \frac{1}{2} \log \left( \frac{\left(1+\left(D+1\right)a\right)^{n-{D}}}{\left(1+Da\right)^{n-{D}-1}} \right) \\ \end{equation} and define the measure $\hat{\mathbb Q}$ by \begin{equation} \frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}:=\exp\left(\hat C-V^{\pi^{*}}_n\right). \end{equation} Clearly, the triplet $(\pi^{*},\hat{\mathbb Q},\hat C)$ satisfies (\ref{2.1}). Thus, in view of Lemma \ref{lem2.1} in order to complete the proof of Theorem \ref{thm1.1} we need to show that $\hat{\mathbb Q}\in\mathcal Q$. Let $X=(S_1-S_0,S_2-S_1,...,S_n-S_{n-1})$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu_n} =(\mu,...,\mu)\in\mathbb R^n$. From (\ref{eq:value}), (\ref{1.5}) and the simple equality $(S_n-S_0)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n X^2_i+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n} X_iX_j$ we have $$V^{\pi^{*} }_n=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left(X (A-I) X{'}+2 \boldsymbol{\mu_n} X'-n a \hat\sigma^2\right).$$ This together with (\ref{2.8-}) and (\ref{2.8+})--(\ref{2.9}) yield $$\frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}:=\frac{\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}X \frac{A}{\sigma^2} X'\right)}{\sqrt {(2\pi)^n | A^{-1}|}}}{\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(X-{\boldsymbol{\mu_n}})\frac{I}{\sigma^2}(X-{\boldsymbol{\mu_n}})'\right)}{\sqrt {(2\pi)^n}}}.$$ Hence, the relation $\left(X;{\mathbb P}\right) \sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol{\mu_n},\sigma^2 I)$ implies that $\hat{\mathbb Q}$ is a probability measure and $\left(X;\hat{\mathbb Q}\right) \sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 A^{-1})$. In particular $\mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[ \log\left(\frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]<\infty$. From Lemma \ref{lem2.2} we obtain that $A^{-1}\in\mathcal S_D$ and so (under the probability measure $\hat{\mathbb Q}$), $X_k$ is independent of $(X_1,...,X_{(k-1-{D})^{+}})$ for all $k$. This yields (\ref{2.0}). Finally, the property $(S_n;\hat{\mathbb Q}) \sim \hat\nu$ follows from Lemma \ref{lem2.3}.
nodes.statement_short: Verification: build $\hat Q$ with density $\exp(\hat C-V^{\pi^*}_n)$, show $X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2A^{-1})$ under it, and use Lemmas 3.2-3.3 to get $\hat Q\in\mathcal Q$.

nodes.name: Constant hat C (2.8+)
nodes.statement: \hat C := \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}n\left(\mu^2-a{\hat\sigma^2}\right) + \frac{1}{2} \log \left( \frac{\left(1+\left(D+1\right)a\right)^{n-{D}}}{\left(1+Da\right)^{n-{D}-1}} \right) \\

nodes.name: Density of hat Q (2.9)
nodes.statement: \frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}:=\exp\left(\hat C-V^{\pi^{*}}_n\right).

nodes.name: Brownian probability space
nodes.statement:
In this section we assume that $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb P)$ is
 a complete
probability space carrying a one-dimensional Brownian motion 
$W=(W_t)_{t \in [0,1]}$ with time horizon $T=1$.

nodes.name: Bachelier model
nodes.statement:
We consider a simple financial market with a riskless savings account bearing
zero interest (for simplicity) and with a risky asset $P$ with Bachelier price
dynamics
${P}_t={P}_0+\theta t+\varsigma W_t, \ \ t\in [0,1]$
 where $P_0\in\mathbb R$ is the initial asset price, $\theta\in\mathbb R$ is the constant
drift and $\varsigma>0$ is the constant volatility.

nodes.name: Constant information delay H
nodes.statement:
We focus on an investor who is informed about the risky asset’s price changes
with a delay $H>0$.

nodes.name: Equidistant trading grid
nodes.statement:
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and consider an investor who can trade and observe the risky asset only at times from the grid
$\left\{0,\frac{1}{n},\frac{2}{n},...,1\right\}$.

nodes.name: Discrete delayed filtration G^n and delay D_n
nodes.statement:
The investor's flow of information is given by the filtration 
$\mathcal G^n_k:=\sigma\left\{P_0,P_{\frac{1}{n}},...,P_{\frac{(k-D_n)\vee 0}{n}}\right\}$, $k=0,1,...,n$ 
where $D_n:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N: m /n\geq H\}=\lceil H n\rceil$.

nodes.name: Static vanilla options priced by hat V
nodes.statement:
In addition, the investor can take a static position in $P_1$, i.e. for any continuous function $f:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R$
 we can buy a vanilla option with the random payoff $f(P_1)$ for the amount $\int f d\hat{\mathcal{V}}$.

nodes.name: Normal pricing measure N(P_0, hat varsigma^2)
nodes.statement:
We assume 
 that $\hat{\mathcal{V}}= \mathcal N(P_0, \hat\varsigma^2)$ 
for some constant $\hat\varsigma>0$.

nodes.name: No-arbitrage in the Bachelier setting
nodes.statement:
As in Section \ref{sec:2}, in order to avoid arbitrage the mean of the distribution 
$\hat{\mathcal{V}}$ should be equal to the initial stock price $P_0$.

nodes.name: Trading strategy on the grid
Piecewise constant strategy (4.0-)
nodes.statement: \gamma_t:=\begin{cases} \gamma_{\frac{k}{n}}, & \text{if \ $\frac{k}{n} \leq t <\frac{k+1}{n}$, \ \ $k=0,1,...,n-2$}\\ \gamma_{\frac{n-1}{n}}, & \text{if \ $\frac{n-1}{n}\leq t\leq 1$} \end{cases}

nodes.name: Set A^n of grid strategies
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal A^n$ the set of all trading strategies.

nodes.name: Terminal portfolio value V_1 (grid)
nodes.statement:
For $\pi=(\gamma,f)\in\mathcal A^n$ the corresponding portfolio value
at the maturity date is given by 
$$
V^{\pi}_1=f(P_1)+\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dP_t -\int fd\hat{\mathcal{V}}.
$$

nodes.name: Stochastic integral of a piecewise constant strategy
nodes.statement:
Observe that for $\gamma$ of the form (\ref{4.0-}) we have 
$\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dP_t=\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma_{\frac{i-1}{n}} \left(P_{\frac{i}{n}}-P_{\frac{i-1}{n}}\right).$

nodes.name: Exponential utility maximization on the grid U_n
Value U_n (4.1)
nodes.statement: U_n(H,\theta,\varsigma,\hat\varsigma):=\sup_{\pi\in\mathcal A^n}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_1\right)\right].

nodes.name: Constant alpha
nodes.statement:
Set 
\begin{equation} \alpha:=\alpha(H,\varsigma,\hat\varsigma)=
 \frac{1}{H}\left(1-\frac{2}{H\frac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}+\sqrt{4(1-H)\frac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}+H^2\frac{\varsigma^4}{\hat\varsigma^4}}}\right).
 \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of alpha (eq:alpha_def)
nodes.statement: \alpha:=\alpha(H,\varsigma,\hat\varsigma)= \frac{1}{H}\left(1-\frac{2}{H\frac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}+\sqrt{4(1-H)\frac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}+H^2\frac{\varsigma^4}{\hat\varsigma^4}}}\right).
nodes.label: eq:alpha_def

nodes.name: Weight function kappa
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa$ equals $\alpha/(1-\alpha H)$ on $[0,H)$ and on each $[kH,(k+1)H)$ is an exponential times a polynomial with recursively defined coefficients $c_k$.

nodes.name: Explicit kappa (eq:b_sol_recursive)
nodes.statement: \kappa_t = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha H} + \sum_{k=1}^{\lceil \frac{1}{H} \rceil - 1} {\mathbb I}_{t \in [kH, (k+1)H)} \exp\big(\alpha\left(t- k H\right)\big) \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} c_{k-j} \frac{(-\alpha)^j}{j!} (t-kH)^{j}
nodes.label: eq:b_sol_recursive

nodes.name: Recurrence for c_k (eq:c_coefficients_recursive)
nodes.statement: c_{k+1} =\exp\left(\alpha H\right)\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_{k-j}\frac{(-\alpha H)^j}{j!} .
nodes.label: eq:c_coefficients_recursive

nodes.name: kappa is well defined
nodes.statement: From (\ref{eq:alpha_def}) we have $\alpha<\frac{1}{H}$ and so $\kappa$ is well defined.
conclusions: From (\ref{eq:alpha_def}) we have $\alpha<\frac{1}{H}$ and so $\kappa$ is well defined.

nodes.name: Derivation of the delay integral equation for kappa
nodes.statement:
The fact that $c_1=-\alpha$ gives 
$\kappa_H=\frac{\alpha^2 H}{1-\alpha H}=\int_{0}^H \kappa_s ds$. 
The recursive definition (\ref{eq:c_coefficients_recursive}) provides that 
$\kappa$ is continuous in the points $2H,3H,...$ and so $\kappa$ is continuous on the interval $[H,1]$. 
From 
(\ref{eq:b_sol_recursive}) and the product rule (for differentiation) we obtain that for any $t\in (kH,(k+1)H)$ 
\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{dt}\kappa_t-\alpha \kappa_t &=-\frac{\alpha^2}{1-\alpha H}
+\exp\big(\alpha\left(t- k H\right)\big) \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} j c_{k-j} \frac{(-\alpha)^j}{j!} (t-kH)^{j-1}\\
&=-\frac{\alpha^2}{1-\alpha H}-\alpha
\exp\big(\alpha\left(t- k H\right)\big) \sum_{j=0}^{k-2} c_{k-1-j} \frac{(-\alpha)^j}{j!} (t-kH)^{j}\\
&=-\alpha\kappa_{t-H}.
\end{align*}

nodes.name: How kappa was obtained
nodes.statement:
In fact our definition of $\kappa$ 
by (\ref{eq:b_sol_recursive})-(\ref{eq:c_coefficients_recursive})
was done after solving explicitly the linear equation (\ref{prop}) with the initial condition 
$\kappa_t=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha H}$ for $t<H$. The solution is obtained recursively. For any $k\in\mathbb N$,
$\kappa_{(kH,(k+1)H}$ solves the simple ordinary differential equation 
$\frac{d}{dt}\kappa_t-\alpha\kappa_t=-\alpha\kappa_{t-H}$ and $\kappa_{t-H}$ is known from previous step. We omit the technical details for this part.
The only details needed are
the definition of $\kappa$ 
by (\ref{eq:b_sol_recursive})-(\ref{eq:c_coefficients_recursive})
and the property (\ref{prop}).

nodes.name: Behaviour of kappa_0 (Figure 1)
nodes.statement:
The initial investment weight in the static option $\kappa_0$ is positive (negative) for $\frac{\hat \varsigma^2}{\varsigma^2} < 1$ ($>1$). Let $\{\mathcal G_t\}_{t=0}^1$ be the augmented filtration which is generated

nodes.name: Continuous-time trading strategy
nodes.statement:
A trading strategy is a 
pair $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ where $\gamma=\left(\gamma_t\right)_{t \in [0,1]}$ is a 
predictable process with respect 
to $(\mathcal G_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ which satisfies $\int_{0}^1 \gamma^2_t dt<\infty$ a.s.

nodes.name: Equivalence of trading strategies (continuous time)
nodes.statement: Similarly to Section \ref{sec:2} we say that two trading strategies $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent if there exists a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $\gamma-\tilde\gamma=c$ $dt\otimes\mathbb P$ a.s and $\tilde f-f$ is a linear function with slope equal to $c$. Clearly if $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ are equivalent then $V^{\pi}_1=V^{\tilde\pi}_1$ a.s. Let us argue that the opposite direction also holds. Indeed, let $\pi=(\gamma,f)$ and $\tilde\pi=(\tilde\gamma,\tilde f)$ be two trading strategies such that $V^{\pi}_1=V^{\tilde\pi}_1$. Set $\beta=\gamma-\tilde\gamma$ and $h=\tilde f-f$. Let $n\in\mathbb N$ such that $\frac{1}{n}<H$. Introduce the process $B_t:=W_{t+1 -\frac{1}{n}}-W_{1-\frac{1}{n}}$, $t\in \left[0,\frac{1}{n}\right]$. From $V^{\pi}_1=V^{\tilde\pi}_1$ we get \begin{equation} h\left(W_{1-\frac{1}{n}}+B_{\frac{1}{n}}\right)=\int_{0}^{1-\frac{1}{n}}\beta_t dW_t+\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}}\beta_{s+1-\frac{1}{n}}dB_s. \end{equation} Observe that $B$ is a Brownian motion which is independent of $\left(W_t\right)_{t\in\left[0,1-\frac{1}{n}\right]}$ and $(\beta_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ (here we use that $\frac{1}{n}<H$). Hence, (\ref{100}) implies that there exists a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $h$ is a linear function with slope equal to $c$ and the restriction of the process $\beta$ to the interval $\left[1-\frac{1}{n},1\right]$ is equal $c$ ($dt\otimes \mathbb P$ a.s.). By repeating this argument for the intervals $\left[\frac{k-1}{n},\frac{k}{n}\right]$, $k=n-1,n-2,...,1$ we conclude that $\beta=c$ $dt\otimes\mathbb P$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Strategies with a.s. equal terminal values differ by a constant position and a linear payoff; shown backwards over intervals of length $1/n<H$.

Indeed, let

Set $\beta=\gamma-\tilde\gamma$ and $h=\tilde f-f$. 
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ such that $\frac{1}{n}<H$.
Introduce the process 
$B_t:=W_{t+1 -\frac{1}{n}}-W_{1-\frac{1}{n}}$, $t\in \left[0,\frac{1}{n}\right]$. From $V^{\pi}_1=V^{\tilde\pi}_1$ we get
\begin{equation} h\left(W_{1-\frac{1}{n}}+B_{\frac{1}{n}}\right)=\int_{0}^{1-\frac{1}{n}}\beta_t dW_t+\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}}\beta_{s+1-\frac{1}{n}}dB_s.
\end{equation}
Observe that
$B$ is a Brownian motion which is independent of $\left(W_t\right)_{t\in\left[0,1-\frac{1}{n}\right]}$ and
$(\beta_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ (here we use that $\frac{1}{n}<H$). Hence, 
(\ref{100}) implies that there exists a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $h$ is a linear
function with slope equal to $c$ and the restriction of the process $\beta$ to the interval

By repeating this argument for the intervals $\left[\frac{k-1}{n},\frac{k}{n}\right]$, $k=n-1,n-2,...,1$
 we conclude that $\beta=c$ $dt\otimes\mathbb P$ as required.

nodes.name: Solution of the continuous-time delayed semistatic hedging problem
nodes.statement: Let $\pi_{*}:=(\Gamma,F)$ where $\Gamma$ is given by (\ref{vol}) and $F(P_1)$ is equal to the right-hand side of (\ref{4.2}). Then, $\pi_{*}$ is the unique (up to equivalency) solution for the optimization problem: $\mbox{Maximize} \ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_1\right)\right] \ \mbox{over} \ \pi\in\mathfrak A. $ Moreover, \begin{align*} &\sup_{\pi\in\mathfrak A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_1\right)\right]= \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi_{*}}_1\right)\right]\\ &=-{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: With delay $H>0$ in continuous time, the limit strategy $(\Gamma,F)$ of Theorem 4.1 is the unique optimizer and the value equals the scaling limit.
assumptions: Let $\pi_{*}:=(\Gamma,F)$ where $\Gamma$ is given by (\ref{vol}) and $F(P_1)$ is equal to the right-hand side of (\ref{4.2})
conclusions: $\pi_{*}$ is the unique (up to equivalency) solution for the optimization problem: $\mbox{Maximize} \ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(- V^{\pi}_1\right)\right] \ \mbox{over} \ \pi\in\mathfrak A. $

Moreover, \begin{align*} &\sup_{\pi\in\mathfrak A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_1\right)\right]= \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi_{*}}_1\right)\right]\\ &=-{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H}. \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm.100

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement: Since the utility function is strictly concave then the optimal portfolio value is unique (if exists). This together with Remark \ref{rem20} gives uniqueness. Next, recall the optimal portfolios $\pi^{*,n}$, $n\in\mathbb N$ from Theorem \ref{thm4.1}. From (\ref{4.3}) it follows that $V^{\pi^{*,n}}\rightarrow V^{\pi_{*}}$ in probability (as $n\rightarrow\infty$). Thus, by applying the Fatou Lemma for the function $x\rightarrow e^{-x}$, we obtain from (\ref{4.0}). $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_1\right)\right]\geq -{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H}.$$ We conclude that in order to complete the proof of Theorem \ref{thm.100} it remains to establish the upper bound \begin{equation} \sup_{\pi\in\mathfrak A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_1\right)\right] \leq -{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H}. \end{equation} This is done in Section \ref{sec:6}.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness from strict concavity and Remark 4.2; lower bound from Theorem 4.1 and Fatou's lemma; the upper bound (9.2) is deferred to Section 5.2.

nodes.name: Upper bound (9.2) for the continuous-time value
nodes.statement: \sup_{\pi\in\mathfrak A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_1\right)\right] \leq -{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H}.
conclusions: \sup_{\pi\in\mathfrak A}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_1\right)\right] \leq -{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H}.

nodes.name: Sign of the investment weights (Figure 2, top)
nodes.statement:
For $\frac{\hat \varsigma^2}{\varsigma^2} < 1$, it holds that $0 < \alpha H < 1$ hence the investment weights $\kappa_t - \kappa_0$ are negative and monotonically decrease with $t$. 
 For $\frac{\hat \varsigma^2}{\varsigma^2} > 1$, we have $\alpha H < 0$ and the investment weights $\kappa_t - \kappa_0$ are positive.

nodes.name: Numerical convergence of n b_i to kappa (Figure 2, bottom)
nodes.statement: As $n$ increases, the discrete values approach the continuous limit, and the curves are barely distinguishable for $n=1000$.

nodes.name: Properties of the limit value U (Figure 3)
nodes.statement:
We observe the following properties:\\
I. For the case where the market pricing rule 
is consistent with the physical measure (i.e. $\varsigma=\hat\varsigma$)
we have $\alpha=0$ and so $U=-1$.\\
II. If $H\downarrow 0$ then 
$\alpha H\rightarrow 1-\frac{\hat\varsigma}{\varsigma}$. Hence, for the case $\varsigma\neq \hat\varsigma$ it holds that
 $\alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2}
{\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\rightarrow -\infty$ and so,
the right hand side of (\ref{4.0}) goes to $0$.
Namely, for vanishing delay $H\downarrow 0$ we have 
an arbitrage opportunity i.e. $U\rightarrow 0$ provided that there is 
inconsistency between the physical measure and the market pricing rule.
Financially speaking,
since the non delayed Bachelier model is complete, then the above inconsistency 
leads to an arbitrage opportunity.\\
III. Since $U(H,\varsigma,\hat\varsigma)$ is a limit value of discrete-time models, then from the discussion
in Section \ref{sec:2} it follows that for a given $H,\varsigma$
the function $U$ is increasing in $\hat\varsigma$ on the interval $[\varsigma,\infty)$ 
and decreasing in $\hat\varsigma$ on the interval $(0,\varsigma)$.
 Moreover, by using the 
the same arguments as in (\ref{static1})--(\ref{static2}) we obtain that 
if $\left |\log\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma}{\varsigma}\right)\right|\rightarrow\infty$ then $U\rightarrow 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Limit value: $U=-1$ when $\varsigma=\hat\varsigma$; $U\to0$ (arbitrage) as $H\downarrow0$ under mispricing; monotone in $\hat\varsigma$ with $U\to 0$ at the extremes.

nodes.name: Vanishing delay and the Merton line
nodes.statement: If $\hat{\varsigma}=\varsigma$ then $\alpha=0$ and so the optimal strategy is $\Gamma\equiv \frac{\theta}{2\varsigma^2}$, $F\equiv 0$ (i.e. the Merton line) and does not depend on the delay $H$. For $\hat{\varsigma}\neq \varsigma$ we observe that the right-hand side of (\ref{4.0}) converges to zero as $H\downarrow 0$. In words, if $\hat{\varsigma}\neq \varsigma$ we obtain an asymptotic arbitrage for vanishing delay. Formally, in this case, $\alpha H \rightarrow 1$ (as $H\downarrow 0$) and so there is a singularity (blow-up) in the optimal trading strategy $\pi_{*}=(\Gamma,F)$. In Figure \ref{fig:kappa_0_vs_H} and Figure \ref{fig:strategy_limit_prop} (Top) we provide additional (numerical) description of the optimal trading strategy $\pi_{*}=(\Gamma,F)$ for a few cases. In addition, Figure \ref{fig:limit_value} displays the limiting value function from \eqref{4.0} as a function of the delay $H$ and the ratio $\frac{\hat\varsigma}{\varsigma}$ for the case of zero drift $(\theta=0)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\hat\varsigma=\varsigma$ the Merton strategy is optimal for every $H$; otherwise the value tends to 0 as $H\downarrow 0$ (asymptotic arbitrage) and the strategy blows up.
nodes.label: rem.new

nodes.name: Discrete Gronwall lemma
nodes.statement: Let a positive real sequence $\{z_j\}_{j=0}^n$ satisfy the recursive relation \begin{equation} z_{j+1}\leq \phi z_j+\psi, \ \ j=0,1...,n-1 \end{equation} for some constants $\phi>1$ and $\psi>0$. Then, $$z_j\leq \frac{\psi}{\phi-1} (\phi^j-1)+\phi^j z_0, \ \ \forall j. $$
assumptions: a positive real sequence $\{z_j\}_{j=0}^n$ satisfy the recursive relation \begin{equation} z_{j+1}\leq \phi z_j+\psi, \ \ j=0,1...,n-1 \end{equation}
conclusions: $$z_j\leq \frac{\psi}{\phi-1} (\phi^j-1)+\phi^j z_0, \ \ \forall j. $$
nodes.label: lem5.1

nodes.name: Proof of the discrete Gronwall lemma
nodes.statement: The proof will be done by induction. For $j=0$ the statement is trivial. Assume the statement holds for $j$, and let us prove it for $j+1$. Indeed, \begin{align*} z_{j+1}&\leq \phi z_j+\psi\\ & \leq \phi \left(\frac{\psi}{\phi-1} (\phi^j-1)+\phi^j z_0\right)+\psi\\ &=\frac{\psi}{\phi-1} (\phi^{j+1}-1)+\phi^{j+1}z_0 \end{align*} and the proof is completed.

nodes.name: O(1/n^C) notation
nodes.statement:
For a constant $C>0$ we use the notation $O\left(1/n^C\right)$ to denote a sequence $\{\alpha_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ which satisfies
$\sup_{n\in\mathbb N} \alpha_n n^C<\infty$.

nodes.name: L^2 convergence of scaled coefficients n b_i to kappa
nodes.statement: For any $n\in\mathbb N$ introduce the function $b^n:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb R$ \begin{equation*} b^n_t:=\begin{cases} n b_{k+1}, & \text{if \ $\frac{k}{n} \leq t <\frac{k+1}{n}$\ \ $k=0,1,...,n-2$}\\ n b_n, & \text{if \ $\frac{n-1}{n}\leq t\leq 1$} \end{cases} \end{equation*} where $\{b_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ is given by (\ref{eq:a_sol})--(\ref{1.4}) for $D=D_n$, $\sigma=\frac{\varsigma}{\sqrt n}$ and $\hat\sigma=\frac{\hat\varsigma}{\sqrt n}$. Then, $$\int_{0}^1 |b^n_t-\kappa_t|^2 dt = O(1/n).$$
nodes.statement_short: The piecewise constant function $b^n_t=n b_{\lfloor nt\rfloor+1}$ built from the discrete coefficients converges to $\kappa$ in $L^2[0,1]$ at rate $O(1/n)$.

Observe that,  egin{align} a_n &:=  rac{\varsigma^2}{2n\hat\varsigma^2}+ rac{\sqrt{\left(2D_n- rac{D^2_n \varsigma^2}{n\hat\varsigma^2}ight)^2- 4 D^2_n \left(1- rac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}ight)}-2D_n}{2 D^2_n}+O(1/n^2)
onumber\ &= \left( rac{\varsigma^2}{2\hat\varsigma^2}- rac{1}{H}+  rac{\sqrt{4 rac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}(1-H)+H^2 rac{\varsigma^4}{\hat\varsigma^4}}}{2 H}ight) rac{1}{n}+O(1/n^2)
onumber\ &=  rac{\alpha}{ (1-\alpha H) } rac{1}{n}+O(1/n^2). \end{align} Next, (ef{1.4}) yields that for any $k\geq D_n-1$ $$b^n_{ rac{k+1}{n}}-b^n_{ rac{k}{n}}= rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\left(b^n_{ rac{k}{n}}-b^n_{ rac{k-D_n}{n}}ight).$$ Thus,  egin{equation} b^n_{ rac{k+1}{n}}=\left(1+ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}ight)b^n_{ rac{k}{n}}-  rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}b^n_{ rac{k-D_n}{n}}, \ \  orall k\geq D_n-1. \end{equation} From (ef{prop}) we have that for any $k\geq D_n$ $$\kappa_{ rac{k+1}{n}}-\kappa_{ rac{k}{n}}= \alpha\left(\int_{ rac{k}{n}}^{ rac{k+1}{n}}\kappa_s ds- \int_{ rac{k}{n}-H}^{ rac{k+1}{n}-H}\kappa_s ds ight).$$ This, together with (ef{4.4}) and the fact that the function $\kappa$ is constant on the interval $[0,H)$ and Lipschitz continuous on the interval $[H,1]$ yield that for any $k\geq D_n$ such that $k
eq 2D_n-1,2 D_n-2$  egin{align*} \kappa_{ rac{k+1}{n}}-\kappa_{ rac{k}{n}}&= rac{\alpha}{n}\left(\kappa_{ rac{k}{n}}-\kappa_{ rac{k-D_n}{n}}ight)+O(1/n^2)\ &= rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\left(\kappa_{ rac{k}{n}}-\kappa_{ rac{k-D_n}{n}}ight)+O(1/n^2). \end{align*} We exclude $k=2D_n-1,2 D_n-2$ because for these $k$ the discontinuity point of $\kappa$ might lie between $ rac{k-D_n}{n}$ and $ rac{k+1}{n}-H$. Namely, $ rac{k-D_n}{n}\leq H\leq  rac{k+1}{n}-H$. We conclude that for any $k\geq D_n$ such that $k
eq 2D_n-1,2 D_n-2$  egin{equation} \kappa_{ rac{k+1}{n}}=\left(1+ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}ight)\kappa_{ rac{k}{n}}-  rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\kappa_{ rac{k-D_n}{n}}+O(1/n^2), \ \  orall k\geq D_n-1. \end{equation} \ ${}$\ 	extbf{Step III:} In this step we complete the proof. We establish (ef{5.10}) by induction on $i$. Observe that $\kappa_H= rac{\alpha^2 H}{1-\alpha H}$ and $b^n_{ rac{D_n-1}{n}}= rac{a^2_n D_n}{a_n D_n+1}$. Thus, from (ef{4.4}) it follows that $\Delta^n_1=O(1/n)$. Assume that the statement holds true for $i$ and let us prove it for $i+1$. Define the sequence (which depends on $n$ and $i$) $$z^{n,i}_j=\left|b^n_{ rac{i D_n+j-1}{n}}-\kappa_{ rac{ i D_n+j}{n}}ight|, \ \ j=0,1,...,D_n\wedge (n-i D_n).$$ Clearly, $z^{n,i}_0\leq \Delta_i$ and so from the induction assumption $z^{n,i}_0= O(1/n)$. From \eqref{5.11},\eqref{5.12} we obtain that for $k<D_n-2$.  egin{align*} z^{n,i}_{k+1} &= \left(1+ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}ight)z^{n,i}_k+ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\left|b^n_{ rac{(i-1) D_n+k-1}{n}}-\kappa_{ rac{(i-1) D_n+k}{n}}ight|+O(1/n^2)\ &=\left(1+ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}ight)z^{n,i}_k+O(1/n^2) \end{align*} where the last equality follows from the fact that $\Delta^n_i=O(1/n)$ (induction assumption) and $ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}=O(1/n)$. We take $k<D_n-2$ only because of the case $i=1$ (recall that in (ef{5.12}) we exclude $k=2D_n-1,2 D_n-2$). Thus, the sequence $\{z^{n,i}_j\}_{j=0}^{D_n-2}$ satisfies the recursive relation (ef{5.rec}) for $\phi=1+ rac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}=1+ rac{\alpha}{n}+O(1/n^2)$ and $\psi=O(1/n^2)$. Hence, from Lemma ef{lem5.1} we obtain that  egin{equation} \max_{0\leq j\leq D_n-2} z^{n,i}_j=O(1/n). \end{equation} It remains to treat the term $z^{n,i}_j$ for $j= D_n-2, D_n-1,D_n$. Once again, since $\kappa$ is constant on the interval $[0,H)$ and Lipschitz continuous on the interval $[H,1]$, then from (ef{4.4}) we have $$\kappa_{ rac{i D_n+j}{n}}= rac{a_n}{a_n D_n+1} \sum_{r=1}^{D_n} \kappa_{ rac{i D_n+j-r}{n}}+O(1/n), \ \ j= D_n-2, D_n-1,D_n.$$ This together with (ef{1.4}), (ef{5.14}) and the induction assumption $\Delta^n_i=O(1/n)$ gives $z^{n,i}_j=O(1/n)$ for $j= D_n-2, D_n-1,D_n$ and the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a sup bound on each delay block; compare the discrete recursion for $b^n$ with the integral equation for $\kappa$ (each with $O(1/n^2)$ error). Induct over blocks of length $D_n$ using the discrete Gronwall lemma.

nodes.name: Blockwise error bound (5.10)
nodes.statement: \Delta^n_i=O(1/n), \ \ \forall i=1,...,\lceil 1/H\rceil

nodes.name: Asymptotics of a_n (4.4)
nodes.statement: a_n &:= \frac{\varsigma^2}{2n\hat\varsigma^2}+\frac{\sqrt{\left(2D_n-\frac{D^2_n \varsigma^2}{n\hat\varsigma^2}\right)^2- 4 D^2_n \left(1-\frac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}\right)}-2D_n}{2 D^2_n}+O(1/n^2)\nonumber\\ &= \left(\frac{\varsigma^2}{2\hat\varsigma^2}-\frac{1}{H}+ \frac{\sqrt{4\frac{\varsigma^2}{\hat\varsigma^2}(1-H)+H^2\frac{\varsigma^4}{\hat\varsigma^4}}}{2 H}\right)\frac{1}{n}+O(1/n^2)\nonumber\\ &= \frac{\alpha}{ (1-\alpha H) }\frac{1}{n}+O(1/n^2).

nodes.name: Recursion for b^n (5.11)
nodes.statement: b^n_{\frac{k+1}{n}}=\left(1+\frac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\right)b^n_{\frac{k}{n}}- \frac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}b^n_{\frac{k-D_n}{n}}, \ \ \forall k\geq D_n-1.

nodes.name: Approximate recursion for kappa (5.12)
nodes.statement: \kappa_{\frac{k+1}{n}}=\left(1+\frac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\right)\kappa_{\frac{k}{n}}- \frac{a_n}{a_nD_n+1}\kappa_{\frac{k-D_n}{n}}+O(1/n^2), \ \ \forall k\geq D_n-1.

nodes.name: Gronwall estimate (5.14)
nodes.statement: \max_{0\leq j\leq D_n-2} z^{n,i}_j=O(1/n).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Choose $n\in\mathbb N$. We apply Theorem \ref{thm1.1} to the sequence $S_k:=P_{k/n}$, $k=0,1...,n$. Thus, let $D=D_n$, $\mu=\frac{\theta}{n}$, $\sigma=\frac{\varsigma}{\sqrt n}$, $\hat\sigma=\frac{\hat\varsigma}{\sqrt n}$. From (\ref{1.6}) and (\ref{4.4}) we obtain \begin{align*} &\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} U_n(H,\mu,\varsigma,\hat\varsigma)\\ &=-\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(na_n\frac{\hat\varsigma^2}{\varsigma^2}-\frac{a_n(n-D_n)}{1+a_n D_n}\right)\right)\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} a_n D_n}}\\ &=-{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{\varsigma^2}+ \alpha\left(\frac{\hat\varsigma^2} {\varsigma^2(1-\alpha H)}+H-1\right)\right)\right)}\sqrt{1-\alpha H} \end{align*} and (\ref{4.0}) follows. Next, by combining (\ref{1.5}) (for the function $f^{*}$) and (\ref{4.4}) we get (\ref{4.2}). Finally, we establish (\ref{4.3}). Set $$\Phi_n=\max_{0\leq k\leq n-1}\left|\gamma^{*,n}_{\frac{k}{n}}-\Gamma_{\frac{k}{n}}\right|, \ \ n\in\mathbb N.$$ The function $\kappa$ is constant on the interval $[0,H)$ and Lipschitz continuous on the interval $[H,1]$ and so, from \cite{Fernique} we obtain that the Volterra Gaussian process $\{\Gamma_t\}_{t=0}^1$ is continuous. Hence (recall that $\gamma^{*,n}$ is piecewise constant), in order to establish (\ref{4.3}) it is sufficient to show that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\Phi_n=0$ a.s. In view of the Borel–Cantelli lemma this will follow from the inequality $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P\left(\Phi_n>\epsilon\right)<\infty, \ \ \forall \epsilon>0.$$ Clearly, the Markov inequality (for $\Phi^6_n$) implies that $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P\left(\Phi_n>\epsilon\right)\leq \frac{1}{\epsilon^6} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\Phi^6_n\right].$$ Thus, it remains to establish the inequality $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\Phi^6_n\right]<\infty.$ To this end we apply Lemma \ref{lem5.2}. Fix $n$. By applying (\ref{1.5}) for $S_k:=P_{k/n}$, $k=0,1...,n$ it follows that $$\gamma^{*,n}_{\frac{k}{n}}=\frac{\theta}{\varsigma^2}+\frac{1}{\varsigma^2}\int_{0}^{k/n}\left(b^n_{\frac{k}{n}-s}-na_n\right)dP_s$$ where $b^n$ and $a_n$ are as before. Thus, from (\ref{vol}), Lemma \ref{lem5.2} and the fact that $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\zeta_s dw_s\sim \mathcal N\left(0,\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\zeta^2_s ds\right)$ for a deterministic $\zeta$ we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\Phi^6_n\right] &\leq \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\left|\gamma^{*,n}_{\frac{k}{n}}-\Gamma_{\frac{k}{n}}\right|^6\right]\\ &=\frac{1}{\varsigma^2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{k/n} \left(\left(b^n_{\frac{k}{n}-s}-na_n\right)-\left(\kappa_{\frac{k}{n}-s}-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha H}\right)\right)dP_s\right|^6\right]\\ &= n O(1/n^3)=O(1/n^2) \end{align*} and the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2.2 on the grid with scaled parameters and take limits using (4.4); for (4.3), Borel-Cantelli with Markov's inequality on sixth moments of Gaussian errors controlled by Lemma 5.2.

nodes.name: Brownian filtration F_t
nodes.statement: Let $\{\mathcal F_t\}_{t=0}^1$, $t\in [0,1]$ be the augmented filtration which is generated by $\{W_t\}_{t=0}^1$.

nodes.name: Zero expectation of delayed stochastic integrals
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon>0$ and $\gamma=(\gamma_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a predictable process with respect to the filtration $\left(\mathcal F_{(t-\epsilon)^{+}}\right)_{t\in [0,1]}$ which satisfies $\int_{0}^1\gamma^2_t dt<\infty$ a.s. If the expectation of the negative part satisfies $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\left(\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_t\right)^{-}\right]<\infty$ then $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_t\right]=0.$
nodes.statement_short: A stochastic integral with an $\epsilon$-delayed integrand whose negative part is integrable has zero mean (no doubling strategies under delay).
assumptions: $\epsilon>0$ and $\gamma=(\gamma_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a predictable process with respect to the filtration $\left(\mathcal F_{(t-\epsilon)^{+}}\right)_{t\in [0,1]}$ which satisfies $\int_{0}^1\gamma^2_t dt<\infty$ a.s.
the expectation of the negative part satisfies $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\left(\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_t\right)^{-}\right]<\infty$
conclusions: $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_t\right]=0.$
nodes.label: lem6.1

nodes.name: Proof by backward induction of zero expectation
nodes.statement: Choose $n\in\mathbb N$ such that $\frac{1}{n}<\epsilon$. Let us prove by backward induction that for any $k=0,1,...,n$ \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^{1} \gamma_t dW_t\left.|\right.\mathcal F_{\frac{k}{n}}\right]= \int_{0}^{\frac{k}{n}}\gamma_t dW_t. \end{equation} For $k=n$ (\ref{6.2}) is obvious. Assume that (\ref{6.2}) is correct for $k$, let us prove it for $k-1$. From the Jensen inequality, the fact that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\left(\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_t\right)^{-}\right]<\infty$ and the induction assumption it follows that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\left(\int_{0}^{\frac{kT}{n}} \gamma_t dW_t\right)^{-}\right]<\infty$ hence the term $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^{\frac{k}{n}} \gamma_t dW_t\left|\right. \mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}\right]$ is well defined. Moreover, the tower property and the induction assumption imply $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^{1} \gamma_t dW_t\left|\right.\mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}\right] =\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^{\frac{k}{n}} \gamma_t dW_t\left.|\right.\mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}\right].$$ Thus, in order to prove (\ref{6.2}) for $k-1$ it remains to establish that \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{\frac{k-1}{n}}^{\frac{k}{n}} \gamma_t dW_t\left|\right. \mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}\right]=0. \end{equation} Indeed, since $\frac{1}{n}<\epsilon$ then $(\gamma_t)_{t\in \left[\frac{k-1}{n},\frac{k}{n}\right]}$ is $\mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}$ measurable, and so, the regular conditions distribution (for details see \cite{shiryaev2016probability}) of $\int_{\frac{k-1}{n}}^{\frac{k}{n}} \gamma_t dW_t$ with respect to $\mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}$ is the normal distribution $\mathcal N\left(0,\int_{\frac{k-1}{n}}^{\frac{k}{n}} \gamma^2_t dt\right)$. Thus, by using (a priori) generalized conditional expectations (as defined in \cite{shiryaev2016probability}) we obtain (\ref{past}). This completes the proof of (\ref{6.2}). Taking $k=0$ in (\ref{6.2}) we obtain $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_t\right]=0.$
nodes.statement_short: Backward induction over a grid of mesh $<\epsilon$: on each interval the integrand is known in advance, so the conditional law of the increment is centered normal.

nodes.name: Martingale property on the grid (6.2)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{0}^{1} \gamma_t dW_t\left.|\right.\mathcal F_{\frac{k}{n}}\right]= \int_{0}^{\frac{k}{n}}\gamma_t dW_t.

nodes.name: Zero conditional increment (past)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_{\frac{k-1}{n}}^{\frac{k}{n}} \gamma_t dW_t\left|\right. \mathcal F_{\frac{k-1}{n}}\right]=0.
nodes.label: past

nodes.name: Lemma fails without delay (doubling strategies)
nodes.statement: Let us notice that for $\epsilon=0$ Lemma \ref{lem6.1} does not hold true. Indeed, the doubling strategies from \cite{harrison1979martingales} are piecewise constant with a (random) finite number of trading times such that the corresponding portfolio value at the maturity date is equal to $1$ almost surely.

nodes.name: Hitsuda representation of equivalent Gaussian measures
nodes.statement:
It is well known (see \cite{H:68}) that for any 
deterministic and measurable function $l_{t,s}$, $0\leq s\leq t\leq 1$ (Volterra kernel) 
belonging to $L^2([0,1]^2)$
there exists a probability measure 
$\mathbb Q(l)\sim\mathbb P$ 
and a process $W^{\mathbb Q(l)}=(W^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ such that 
$W^{\mathbb Q(l)}$ is a $\mathbb Q(l)$-Brownian motion and we have the equality
\begin{equation} W^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t=W_t+\int_{0}^t\int_{0}^s l_{s,u} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_u ds, \ \ t\in [0,1].
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Every square-integrable Volterra kernel $l$ gives an equivalent measure $\mathbb Q(l)$ under which $W$ plus a Volterra drift is a Brownian motion.
assumptions:
for any 
deterministic and measurable function $l_{t,s}$, $0\leq s\leq t\leq 1$ (Volterra kernel) 
belonging to $L^2([0,1]^2)$
conclusions:
there exists a probability measure 
$\mathbb Q(l)\sim\mathbb P$ 
and a process $W^{\mathbb Q(l)}=(W^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ such that 
$W^{\mathbb Q(l)}$ is a $\mathbb Q(l)$-Brownian motion and we have the equality
\begin{equation}\label{gir}
W^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t=W_t+\int_{0}^t\int_{0}^s l_{s,u} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_u ds, \ \ t\in [0,1].
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Hitsuda representation (gir)
nodes.statement: W^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t=W_t+\int_{0}^t\int_{0}^s l_{s,u} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_u ds, \ \ t\in [0,1].
nodes.label: gir

nodes.name: Density of Q(l)
nodes.statement:
From the Girsanov theorem 
$$\frac{d\mathbb Q(l)}{d\mathbb P}=\exp\left(-\int_{0}^1 \int_{0}^t l_{t,s} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_sdW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t+
\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\left(\int_{0}^t l_{t,s} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_s\right)^2 dt\right). $$
conclusions:
From the Girsanov theorem 
$$\frac{d\mathbb Q(l)}{d\mathbb P}=\exp\left(-\int_{0}^1 \int_{0}^t l_{t,s} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_sdW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_t+
\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\left(\int_{0}^t l_{t,s} dW^{\mathbb Q(l)}_s\right)^2 dt\right). $$

nodes.name: Relative entropy of Q(l)
nodes.statement:
Hence, 
from the It\^{o} Isometry and the Fubini theorem
we obtain that the relative entropy is given by 
\begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q(l)}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q(l)}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]
=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\int_{0}^t l^2_{t,s}ds dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\int_{s}^1 l^2_{t,s}dt ds.
\end{equation}
conclusions:
Hence, 
from the It\^{o} Isometry and the Fubini theorem
we obtain that the relative entropy is given by 
\begin{equation}\label{2+.entropy}
\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q(l)}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q(l)}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]
=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\int_{0}^t l^2_{t,s}ds dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\int_{s}^1 l^2_{t,s}dt ds.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Relative entropy formula (2+.entropy)
nodes.statement: \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q(l)}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q(l)}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right] =\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\int_{0}^t l^2_{t,s}ds dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^1\int_{s}^1 l^2_{t,s}dt ds.
nodes.label: 2+.entropy

nodes.name: Kernel class Gamma_epsilon
nodes.statement:
For any $\epsilon>0$ denote by $\Gamma_{\epsilon}$ the set of all deterministic, measurable and bounded functions $l_{t,s}$, $0\leq s\leq t\leq 1$ 
such that $l_{t,s}=0$ if $t>s+H-\epsilon $ and
\begin{equation} \int_{0}^1\left(1-\int_{s}^1 l_{t,s} dt\right)^2 ds=\hat{\varsigma}^2.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma_\epsilon$: bounded deterministic Volterra kernels vanishing for $t>s+H-\epsilon$ whose induced terminal variance is $\hat\varsigma^2$.

nodes.name: Variance constraint (variance)
nodes.statement: \int_{0}^1\left(1-\int_{s}^1 l_{t,s} dt\right)^2 ds=\hat{\varsigma}^2.
nodes.label: variance

nodes.name: Proof of the upper bound (9.2)
nodes.statement:
The proof will be done in three steps. \ ${}$\ 	extbf{Step I:} We start with reducing the proof to the special case where $P_0=	heta=0$ and $\varsigma=1$, i.e. $P=W$. By considering the map $Pightarrow  rac{P-P_0}{\varsigma}$ and $\mathcal N(P_0, \hat{\varsigma}^2)ightarrow \mathcal N\left(0,  rac{\hat{\varsigma}^2}{\varsigma^2}ight)$ it follows that if (ef{9.2}) holds true for the case $P_0=0$ and $\varsigma=1$ then it holds for the general case. Thus, it remains to treat the drift $	heta$. Assume that $P_0=0$, $\varsigma=1$ and introduce the probability measure $	ilde{\mathbb P}$ by $ rac{d	ilde{\mathbb P}}{d\mathbb P}:=\exp\left(-	heta P_T+ rac{	heta^2}{2}ight).$ From the Girsanov theorem it follows that $P$ is a standard Brownian motion under $	ilde{\mathbb P}$. This property together with the simple equality $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{{\gamma,f}}_1ight)ight]= \exp\left(- rac{	heta^2}{2} ight)\mathbb E_{	ilde{\mathbb P}}\left[-\exp\left(-V^{{\gamma-	heta,f}}_Tight)ight] \ \  orall (\gamma,f)\in\mathfrak A $$ yield that if Theorem (ef{9.2}) holds true for $P=W$ then it holds true for the case of constant drift as well. Hence from now on we assume that $P=W$. \ ${}$\ 	extbf{Step II:} Let $\epsilon>0$. In this step we prove that for any $l\in\Gamma_{\epsilon}$ and $\pi\in\mathfrak A$ with $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_1ight)ight]<\infty$ we have $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q(l)}[V^{\pi}_1]=0.$ Choose $l\in\Gamma_{\epsilon}$, $\pi\in\mathfrak A$ with $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_1ight)ight]<\infty$ and denote $\mathbb Q:=\mathbb Q(l)$. From the Fubini theorem and (ef{gir}) it follows that $W_1=\int_{0}^1\left(1-\int_{s}^1 l_{t,s}dtight)dW^{\mathbb Q}_s.$ This together with (ef{variance}) imply that $(W_1;\mathbb Q) \sim \hat{\mathcal V}$. Let us show that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\left(\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_tight)^{-}ight]<\infty$. Indeed, in view of the relations $\int f d \hat{\mathcal V}<\infty$ and $(W_1;\mathbb Q) \sim \hat{\mathcal V}$ we have $f(W_T)\in L^1(\mathbb Q)$ and  egin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} [f(W_1)]=\int f d \hat{\mathcal V}. \end{equation} From the classical Legendre-Fenchel duality inequality $xy \leq e^x + y(\log y-1)$ for $x=\left(V^{\pi}_1ight)^{-}$ and $y= rac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}$ we obtain $ \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\left(V^{\pi}_1ight)^{-}ight]\leq \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_1ight)ight]+ \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left( rac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}ight)ight] <\infty. $ This together with (ef{6+.3}) yield $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\left(\int_{0}^1 \gamma_t dW_tight)^{-}ight]<\infty$. Finally, $$\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\int_{0}^1\gamma_t dW_tight]= \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\int_{0}^1\left(\gamma_s-\int_{s}^{s\vee\left(s+H-\epsilonight)}\gamma_t l_{t,s}dtight) dW^{\mathbb Q}_sight]=0.$$ The first equality follows from the Fubini theorem and the fact that $l\in\Gamma_{\epsilon}$. for any $\mathbb Q\in\mathcal Q$ 
\begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[V^{\pi}_n]=0.

Indeed, let $\pi\in\mathcal A$ be as above and 
$\mathbb Q\in\mathcal Q$. In view of the relations 
$\int |f| d\hat\nu<\infty$ and $(S_n;\mathbb Q) \sim \hat\nu$ we have 
$f(S_n)\in L^1(\mathbb Q)$ and 
\begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} [f(S_n)]=\int f d\hat\nu. 
\end{equation}

from the classical Legendre-Fenchel duality inequality
$xy \leq e^x + y(\log y-1)$ for $x=\left(V^{\pi}_n\right)_{-}$ (as usual we set $z_{-}:=-\min(0,z)$) 
and 
$y=\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}$ we obtain 
\begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\left(V^{\pi}_n\right)_{-}\right]\leq 
\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_n\right)\right]+
\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]
<\infty.
\end{equation}

$\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma_i X_i\right)_{-}\right]<\infty$.

 $\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma_i X_i\right]=0$.

\textbf{Step II:}
We proceed using similar arguments to those in Step II of the proof of Theorem $1.1$ in \cite{dolinsky2023exponential}.
From (\ref{2.1})--(\ref{2.2}) for $\pi:=\tilde\pi$ we obtain
\begin{equation} \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\tilde \pi}_n\right)\right] \right)=-C=- \mathbb E_{\tilde{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log
\left(\frac{d\tilde{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right].
\end{equation}
Next, it is well known that for a strictly concave utility maximization problem, the 
optimal portfolio value is unique (if exists) and so in view of Remark \ref{rem2} and 
(\ref{2.5}), in order to complete the proof of the Lemma it remains to show that in general we have the inequality
\begin{equation} \log\left(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\pi}_n\right)\right] \right)\geq -\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log\left(\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right] \ \ \forall (\pi,\mathbb Q)\in\mathcal A\times\mathcal Q.
\end{equation}
Let us establish (\ref{2.6}).
We assume that $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_n\right)\right]<\infty$ (otherwise (\ref{2.6}) is trivial). Then
for any $z\geq 0$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_n\right)\right]
&=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \pi}_n\right)+z \frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}V^{\pi}_n\right]\\
&\geq \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[z\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\left(1-\log
\left(z\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right)\right]\\
&=z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log
\left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right].
\end{align*}

The inequality follows from the Legendre-Fenchel duality
inequality $xy \leq e^x+y(\log y-1)$ by setting $x=-V^{\pi}_n$ and 
$y=z\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}$.
The last equality is straightforward. 
From simple calculus it follows that the concave function 
$z\rightarrow z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log
\left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]$, $z>0$ attains its maximum at $z^{*}:=\exp\left(-\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[\log
\left(\frac{d{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]\right)$ and the corresponding maximal value 
is also $z^{*}$. This completes the proof of (\ref{2.6}).
